title: Clinical Trial Efficacy and Safety Analysis
text:
This report presents a reproducible efficacy and safety analysis using the publicly available CDISC ADaM Pilot 01 clinical trial data.
The analysis included 254 participants:

86 assigned to placebo;
84 assigned to Xanomeline High Dose; and
84 assigned to Xanomeline Low Dose.

Neither Xanomeline dose demonstrated a statistically significant adjusted efficacy difference compared with placebo at Week 24.
Treatment-emergent adverse events were more frequent in both Xanomeline groups than in the placebo group. Study discontinuation was also substantially higher, while Week 24 completion was lower, in both active treatment groups.
Overall, the findings suggest an uncertain efficacy signal accompanied by a less favourable tolerability profile for Xanomeline.

title: Clinical Trial Efficacy and Safety Analysis
text:
Data source
The analysis used publicly available CDISC ADaM Pilot 01 datasets.
The principal analysis datasets were:

ADSL for participant-level information and treatment assignment;
ADQSADAS for ADAS-Cog(11) efficacy assessments; and
ADAE for adverse-event analyses.

Raw data were imported and processed in earlier project notebooks. Notebook 5 uses the analysis outputs created by those notebooks.

title: Clinical Trial Efficacy and Safety Analysis
text:
Analysis populations
The baseline and efficacy analyses included the 254 randomised participants represented in the subject-level analysis dataset.
The safety analysis used participants included in the safety population and their actual treatment assignments.

title: Clinical Trial Efficacy and Safety Analysis
text:
Efficacy endpoint
The efficacy endpoint was the ADAS-Cog(11) total score.
Higher ADAS-Cog(11) scores indicate greater cognitive impairment. Therefore, an increase from baseline represents worsening, while a negative active-treatment difference relative to placebo numerically favours Xanomeline.

title: Clinical Trial Efficacy and Safety Analysis
text:
Statistical methods
Continuous baseline variables were summarised using medians and interquartile ranges. Categorical variables were summarised using counts and percentages.
The adjusted Week 24 efficacy model included:

treatment group;
baseline ADAS-Cog(11) score;
age; and
sex.

Placebo was used as the reference treatment.
Adjusted treatment effects are presented with standard errors, 95% confidence intervals, and exploratory p-values.
Safety outcomes were summarised as the number and percentage of participants with at least one event.

title: Clinical Trial Efficacy and Safety Analysis
text:
ADAS-Cog(11) trajectory
The following figure presents the unadjusted mean ADAS-Cog(11) score over time by treatment group.








Figure 1: Mean ADAS-Cog(11) score over time by treatment group.





Mean ADAS-Cog(11) scores increased over time in all treatment groups, indicating worsening cognitive performance.
The raw trajectory should not be interpreted as an adjusted treatment comparison because treatment groups differed slightly in their baseline scores.

For Xanomeline High Dose versus placebo, the adjusted difference was −1.085 points, with a 95% confidence interval from −2.627 to 0.458 and a p-value of 0.167.
For Xanomeline Low Dose versus placebo, the adjusted difference was −0.541 points, with a 95% confidence interval from −2.070 to 0.988 and a p-value of 0.486.
Both adjusted estimates numerically favoured Xanomeline because they were negative. However, both confidence intervals included zero, and neither comparison was statistically significant.
The analysis therefore did not provide conclusive evidence of a Week 24 treatment effect for either Xanomeline dose.

At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in:

75.6% of placebo participants;
90.5% of Xanomeline High Dose participants; and
91.7% of Xanomeline Low Dose participants.

Possibly or probably treatment-related events occurred in:

50.0% of placebo participants;
83.3% of Xanomeline High Dose participants; and
85.7% of Xanomeline Low Dose participants.

At least one severe treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in:

5.8% of placebo participants;
9.5% of Xanomeline High Dose participants; and
19.0% of Xanomeline Low Dose participants.

These findings indicate a less favourable adverse-event profile for both Xanomeline treatment groups.

Study discontinuation occurred in:

Discontinuation was therefore more than twice as frequent in both Xanomeline groups as in the placebo group.
The available adverse-event data did not support determining which study discontinuations were specifically caused by an adverse event because the adverse-event action variable was missing.

title: AWS Deployment
text:
Overview
This notebook documents the deployment of the final CDISC ADaM Pilot 01 clinical trial report as a static website using Amazon Simple Storage Service, or Amazon S3.
The analytical work and final report were created locally using R and Quarto. The rendered, self-contained HTML report was then deployed to Amazon S3 for public portfolio access.


Deployment architecture
The deployment workflow was:

Analysis datasets were processed in R.
Tables and figures were generated in R.
Quarto rendered the final report as a self-contained HTML file.
The report was copied and renamed to index.html.
The file was uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Static website hosting was enabled for the bucket.
Public read access was configured for the website object.
The S3 website endpoint was tested in a web browser.



Local report preparation


Code
library(here)

report_path <- here(
  "reports",
  "r",
  "05_final_report.html"
)

file.exists(report_path)

AWS service
Amazon S3 was used to host the final static HTML report.
A general-purpose S3 bucket was created for this portfolio project. The self-contained report was uploaded as index.html, and static website hosting was configured with index.html as the index document.
The deployment used only public-read permission for the hosted report. No AWS access keys, passwords, or confidential data were stored in the project repository.


Deployed asset
The deployed website contains the final integrated clinical report, including:

study background and objectives;
analysis methods;
adjusted efficacy results;
treatment-emergent adverse-event summaries;
discontinuation and completion summaries;
data-quality observations;
limitations; and
conclusions.

Because Quarto embedded the figures, styles, and supporting resources in the final HTML document, only one report file was required for the basic S3 deployment.


Validation
Deployment validation included:

confirming the local report existed;
confirming the copied index.html existed;
comparing local and deployment file sizes;
confirming the object was uploaded to S3;
opening the S3 static website endpoint;
checking table-of-contents navigation;
confirming all tables rendered;
confirming both figures rendered; and
testing the website in a separate browser window.



Security considerations
Only public portfolio outputs were deployed.
The following items were not uploaded:

raw credentials;
AWS access keys;
local R session files;
confidential data;
project source datasets; and
files containing personal or sensitive information.



Limitations
The basic Amazon S3 website endpoint does not provide the same security and custom-domain features as a production website deployment.
A future enhancement could use Amazon CloudFront to provide HTTPS, caching, and a secure distribution in front of a private S3 bucket.


Conclusion
The project demonstrates an end-to-end workflow covering clinical data analysis, reproducible reporting, and cloud-based publication.
R and Quarto were used to create the analytical outputs and report, while Amazon S3 was used to deploy the final report as a static website.
